key_insight: Human and LLM-generated synthesis recipes performed similarly across known and unknown materials, and their closed-loop collaboration enabled discovery of a new material, Ba3PtO5.
engineering_relevance: The study shows that pairing LLMs with experimental feedback can accelerate materials synthesis planning and expand discovery in structured chemical families.
method: Generated synthesis recipes for known and candidate new materials using both humans and LLMs.
Tested recipes in the lab and fed success/failure results back into a closed-loop collaboration.
Focused on the Ruddlesden-Popper homologous series to probe a well-studied yet discovery-rich materials space.
evidence_signal: Experimental success rates were comparable between humans and LLMs, with known-material synthesis near 75–83% in round one and unknown-material synthesis much lower at 14–22% across rounds.
watch_item: Results are specific to one homologous materials family, so generalization to broader chemistry and more complex synthesis routes remains uncertain.
paper_title: Human and LLM Collaboration for Accelerated Materials Synthesis and Discovery
